teaser: An ad for cigarette paper so beautiful that people wanted it on their walls.
review_notes:
Dimensions given as about 66.7 x 46.4 cm for the 1896 edition: check against the copy used.
Story that collectors bribed bill posters or cut Mucha posters off walls at night is widely repeated for Gismonda, stated here in general terms.
Critics' nickname 'macaroni' for Mucha's hair: commonly reported.
JOB name origin (initials J B of Jean Bardou with a diamond read as O): standard account.
The smoke is described as pale and silvery from this reproduction; some impressions use metallic ink, not claimed here.

lesson.text: This is a sheet of paper made to sell sheets of paper. It measures about 67 by 46 cm (26 by 18 in), it was printed in Paris in 1896 by the thousands, and it was meant to be glued to a wall and rained on. The product: JOB, a brand of thin papers for rolling your own cigarettes.

The man who drew it, Alphonse Mucha, was a Czech illustrator who had been scraping by in Paris for years. Then, in the last days of 1894, he designed a theater poster for the star actress Sarah Bernhardt. It went up on January 1, 1895. Within weeks all of Paris knew his name, and every company wanted a “Mucha woman” of its own.
Mucha's posters were so desired that collectors reportedly bribed the men who pasted them up, or slipped out at night with a razor to cut them off the walls before the glue dried.

So how do you make a square of cigarette paper look desirable? Mucha barely shows it. He shows what it feels like instead. Follow the smoke from the tip of the cigarette upward, and watch what the woman's face is doing.

lesson.title: Selling a feeling
lesson.text: Three stops: the product, the pleasure, and the trail between them.

spots.title: The cigarette
spots.text: The whole product is this small white stick, held loosely between thumb and finger. One red dot marks the glowing tip. It is the only thing in the poster you could actually buy.

spots.title: Eyes closed
spots.text: Her head tilts back, eyelids lowered, lips slightly parted. She is not looking at you or selling you anything. She is simply enjoying herself, and you are allowed to watch.

spots.title: The smoke
spots.text: A pale, silvery ribbon rises from the cigarette, folds over itself and drifts across the big letters. Mucha draws smoke as if it were silk.

lesson.text: That closed-eyed pleasure was a provocation. In 1896 a respectable woman did not smoke in public, and she certainly did not let her hair fall loose over a bare shoulder while doing it. Mucha's smoker is free, a little scandalous, and completely at ease. The brand borrowed her nerve.

The name itself is an accident. The founder, Jean Bardou of Perpignan in southern France, stamped his papers with his initials, J and B, separated by a small diamond. Customers read the diamond as an O and asked for “JOB.” The company gave in and kept the name. Mucha did not stop at the three giant letters.
The brand name is hidden many more times in the violet background, as a small interlaced monogram. Can you tap one?

spots.title: The monograms
spots.text: Thin green lines weave J, O and B into a star-like knot, repeated like wallpaper. You absorb the name a dozen times without reading it once: an early lesson in branding.

lesson.text: Now the hair, the part everyone remembers. It does not fall, it travels: thick strands split, curl back and tie themselves into loops, more like vines or wrought iron than anything a comb has touched. This taste for long, whipping, plant-like curves is the signature of Art Nouveau, the “new art” that swept Europe around 1900.
Critics of the day joked that Mucha's women had heads full of macaroni. The nickname stuck, and so did the hairstyle: in Paris, Art Nouveau was often simply called “le style Mucha.”

The poster is a color lithograph. The artist draws with a greasy crayon on a flat slab of limestone, the stone is wetted, and oily ink sticks only where the crayon went. Each color needs its own stone, and the same sheet passes through the press once per color. A few flat tones and a dark outline were all Mucha needed.

spots.title: Berries and a jewel
spots.text: The poster's only bright red besides her lips and the cigarette tip: a spray of beads and a round clasp pinned in her hair. A tiny accent that keeps pulling your eye back to the head.

spots.title: Hair as ornament
spots.text: Here the strands stop behaving like hair. They cross, loop and knot in flat ribbons with a firm outline, the “macaroni” that critics teased.

spots.title: Breaking the frame
spots.text: The curls spill over the patterned border instead of stopping at it. The figure seems to sit in front of the poster rather than inside it.

spots.title: A paper mosaic
spots.text: The border is drawn as tiny tiles set in zigzags, like the mosaics of a Byzantine church. Mucha gives a cigarette ad the trappings of a sacred image.

spots.title: The O
spots.text: The middle letter circles behind her head like a halo, a device Mucha used again and again to crown his women.

spots.title: Signed
spots.text: “Mucha,” underlined, in the lower right. Printers rarely let designers sign so visibly. By 1896 his name was part of what the client was paying for.

lesson.text: Mucha understood that an advertisement sells a mood, not an object. Dreamy face, flowing line, a name repeated until it sinks in: the recipe is still in use.

Mucha came to resent being known for posters. From 1910 he spent nearly two decades on the Slav Epic, twenty enormous canvases about the history of the Slavic peoples, which he considered his real life's work.

History has been stubborn about it. The epic hangs in the Czech Republic, admired by those who make the trip. The woman with the cigarette is on dorm walls, tin boxes and tote bags all over the world, still half asleep in her cloud of smoke.

quiz.question: What product does this poster advertise?
quiz.explanation: JOB was a brand of thin papers for rolling your own cigarettes.

quiz.question: Where does the name JOB come from?
options: The initials J and B with a diamond read as an O
quiz.explanation: Jean Bardou's initials were separated by a diamond that customers read as an O.

quiz.question: What made Mucha famous almost overnight?
options: A theater poster for Sarah Bernhardt
quiz.explanation: His poster for the actress went up on January 1, 1895, and Paris noticed at once.

quiz.question: In lithography, what does each color require?
options: Its own stone and its own pass through the press
quiz.explanation: Each color is printed from a separate limestone slab onto the same sheet.

quiz.question: What did critics compare the hair of Mucha's women to?
quiz.explanation: The looping, ribbon-like strands earned the joking nickname macaroni.

facts.text: The brand name appears only once on the poster, in the three large letters.
facts.explanation: Small JOB monograms are repeated all over the violet background.

facts.text: In 1896, a woman smoking in public was considered daring.
facts.explanation: Respectable women did not smoke in public, which gave the image its edge.

facts.text: Mucha considered his posters his most important work.
facts.explanation: He regarded the Slav Epic, twenty huge history paintings, as his real life's work.
